o: For each employee, count pairs of shifts that overlap, where an earlier-starting shift overlaps a later one if its end_time is strictly after the later shift's start_time. Only employees with at least one overlapping pair appear. In the sample, employee 1 has pairs (08-12, 11-15) and (11-15, 14-18) giving 2, employee 3 has none and is excluded.
k: Order the pair by start_time so each overlapping pair is counted once.
Condition: s1.start_time < s2.start_time AND s1.end_time > s2.start_time.
An inner join with GROUP BY naturally drops employees with zero overlaps.

a.i: Join the table to itself on employee_id, requiring the first shift to start strictly earlier and to end strictly after the second shift starts. Grouping by employee and counting joined rows yields the number of overlapping pairs; employees without overlaps produce no rows and are absent, as required.
s: Self-join EmployeeShifts s1, s2 on employee_id.
Filter s1.start_time < s2.start_time AND s1.end_time > s2.start_time.
GROUP BY employee_id, COUNT(*) as overlapping_shifts, ORDER BY employee_id.

c.python:
SELECT s1.employee_id,
       COUNT(*) AS overlapping_shifts
FROM EmployeeShifts s1
JOIN EmployeeShifts s2
  ON s1.employee_id = s2.employee_id
 AND s1.start_time < s2.start_time
 AND s1.end_time > s2.start_time
GROUP BY s1.employee_id
ORDER BY s1.employee_id;

a.t: O(S²) per employee in the worst case due to the self-join

w: Strict inequalities match the definition ('later than'), so touching shifts (end == next start) do not count. The (employee_id, start_time) key guarantees no duplicate pairs. A follow-up: find the maximum number of concurrently active shifts — that needs a sweep with SUM over ordered events rather than pair counting.
